newsitem.title: USA: Simpson case casts shadow over L.A. election.
newsitem.headline: Simpson case casts shadow over L.A. election.

text.p: The specter of the O.J. Simpson murder case hangs over next week's election for Los Angeles County district attorney.
Unless he can shed the sobriquet "the man who lost the Simpson trial," Gil Garcetti risks not being re-elected on November 5 to a second four-year term.

Even as Simpson's civil trial was taking place, Garcetti, who became America's best-known district attorney last year under the intense media spotlight of Simpson's criminal trial, was facing a challenge from one of his own deputies, John Lynch.
At the March primary Garcetti was forced into a runoff election after he picked up only 37 percent of the vote to Lynch's 21 percent.

Lynch was hammered in his campaign about the apparent inability of the district attorney's office under Garcetti to win big cases such as the Simpson murder trial. Garcetti countered by portraying Lynch as an insensitive bureaucrat, uninterested in issues like spousal and child abuse that Garcetti championed.
And in recent TV ads he turned the tables on Lynch, and the war of words has turned nastier.
Garcetti pointed to his challenger's apparent mishandling of several other well-publicized trials, including the prosecution of savings-and-loan chief Charles Keating.
Garcetti's ad concluded Lynch is "too risky to be D.A."

Lynch branded the spots "sleazy" and "a pathetic attempt to scare people," pointing out that he won Keating's conviction on fraud charges and that the case was overturned only because of faulty jury instructions by the judge.
"For 10 months this campaign has been about Gil," said Garcetti's campaign manager Matt Middlebrook. "Now John's getting hot under the collar because all of a sudden it's about him."
But it is the Simpson case that haunts Garcetti.

Simpson was acquitted on October 3, 1995, in the murders of his ex-wife and a friend, despite what Garcetti said was a "mountain of evidence." The former football star was on trial this week in a civil wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.
During debates with Lynch Garcetti defended his record. "We convinced about 80 percent of the people of this country about the guilt of that defendant," he said.
Lynch responded by saying: "The only verdict that matters is those 12 people in the jury box. Those people, somehow, were not convinced."

In addition to losing the case Garcetti earned the wrath of other staff in his office for giving big bonuses to the high-profile lawyers who unsuccessfully prosecuted Simpson -- Marcia Clark, Christopher Darden and William Hodgman.
Garcetti also received criticism after two separate juries were deadlocked in the murder trials of the Erik and Lyle Menendez, who shotgunned their wealthy parents in their Beverly Hills home.
The brothers were convicted at a second trial this year and given life sentences.
And a string of other high-profile losses have dogged Garcetti since he succeeded Ira Reiner in 1992:

-- Four white police officers were acquitted in state court of beating black motorist Rodney King after they were captured on videotape raining blows on him. The acquittal sparked deadly street riots in Los Angeles, and two of the men were later convicted in federal court.
-- A year-long child molestation investigation against pop star Michael Jackson ended in 1994 with no charges filed.
-- Rap star Snoop Doggy Dogg and his bodyguard were acquitted of murder earlier this year.

Erwin Chemerinsky, a law professor at the University of Southern California, said, "I think it is unfair to evaluate (him) solely on his handling of one case. He should be evaluated on the basis of how he runs the office and not on one atypical case."
"Overall he's done a very good job, although some things have occurred that troubled me," he said without specifying.
"Unfortunately I think people will vote on the basis of the Simpson case," said Chemerinsky.
